clinical_knowledge.topic: Corneal abrasion (fingernail trauma) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Corneal abrasion (fingernail trauma) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Corneal Abrasion finger: Fluorescein stain check, topical Erythromycin ointment, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe sharp pain, tearing, photophobia post-scratch

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe sharp pain, tearing, photophobia post-scratch. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Corneal Abrasion finger.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Corneal abrasion (fingernail trauma).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Corneal foreign body without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Whitish infiltrate would suggest secondary infection.
management_principles: Plan for Corneal Abrasion finger: Fluorescein stain check, topical Erythromycin ointment
Urgently refer for reduced vision, irregular pupil, hyphema, suspected penetrating injury, corneal infiltrate, or failure to improve
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.
